name: The Lemons Problem
statement: When buyers cannot tell good from bad, sellers of good goods leave, and the market fills with junk.
statementAccent: sellers of good goods leave, and the market fills with junk
meaning: The lemons problem, from George Akerlof's landmark 1970 paper The Market for Lemons, analyses how asymmetric information, where sellers know more about a product's quality than buyers, can cause markets to fail through adverse selection. In the used-car market Akerlof used to illustrate it, bad cars are lemons and good ones are sometimes called peaches or cherries. Sellers know which is which, but buyers cannot tell them apart, so buyers will pay only a price reflecting average quality. At that average price, owners of good cars refuse to sell below their cars' true worth and withdraw, which lowers the average quality of what remains, pushing the price down further, in a downward spiral that can shrink or unravel the market. The paper, initially rejected by several journals, became foundational to information economics and contributed to Akerlof's 2001 Nobel Memorial Prize, shared with Michael Spence and Joseph Stiglitz.
mechanism: The failure arises because buyers cannot observe quality before purchase and so cannot pay more for a good item than for a bad one; they rationally offer only what an average-quality item is worth. This average price is too low to compensate sellers of high-quality goods, who therefore leave the market, taking their good items with them. Their departure lowers the average quality of the remaining pool, which justifies an even lower price, which drives out the next-best sellers, and so on. Good products are progressively driven out by bad, an adverse-selection spiral that Akerlof explicitly likened to Gresham's law, that bad money drives out good. In the extreme, the market can collapse entirely, with no trades occurring even though mutually beneficial trades in high-quality goods would exist if quality were observable. The core problem is the information asymmetry, and remedies work by reducing it or by letting quality be credibly signalled or verified.

examples.text: Buyers pay only average-quality prices, so owners of good used cars withdraw, the average quality falls, and the price drops further in a spiral.
Good products are progressively driven out by bad, which Akerlof compared to Gresham's law, that bad money drives out good.
Sellers overcome the problem with warranties, brands, reputation, certification, and signalling, which credibly convey quality to buyers.

variants.name: Adverse selection
variants.text: The general phenomenon that when quality is hidden and buyers pay average prices, high-quality participants exit, degrading the pool that remains.

variants.name: Signalling and screening
variants.text: The complementary responses, developed by Spence and Stiglitz, in which informed parties signal quality or uninformed parties screen to elicit it.

whyItMatters: The lemons problem is a foundational contribution to information economics, showing that asymmetric information alone can cause markets to malfunction or collapse even when willing buyers and sellers of good products exist. It reframed how economists think about markets, moving beyond the assumption of full information to explain a wide range of real phenomena: adverse selection in insurance, where the least healthy are most eager to buy; difficulties in credit and labour markets, where quality is hard to observe; and the design of institutions, from warranties and brands to certification, licensing, and online reputation systems, that exist precisely to overcome information gaps. Alongside Michael Spence's work on signalling and Joseph Stiglitz's on screening, it earned Akerlof a share of the 2001 Nobel Memorial Prize and helped establish the economics of information as a central field.

working.text: let sellers know product quality while buyers cannot distinguish good from bad before purchase.
note that buyers rationally pay only what average quality is worth, too little for owners of good items.
see good sellers exit, average quality fall, price drop further, and the market shrink or collapse unless information is restored.

limits: The lemons problem shows what can happen under asymmetric information, not what must happen; in practice, institutions frequently overcome it. Warranties, guarantees, brands, reputation, certification, licensing, and signalling and screening mechanisms all reduce the information gap and let quality trades proceed, which is why many used-car and other markets function rather than collapse. The model is a stylised illustration, assuming buyers cannot verify quality at all and sellers know it perfectly, whereas reality lies between these extremes. Signalling and screening, the remedies associated with Spence and Stiglitz, are complementary contributions rather than parts of Akerlof's original paper. So the lemons problem identifies a genuine tendency toward market breakdown that asymmetric information creates, while the prevalence of countermeasures explains why so many such markets survive.
misreadings: The lemons problem does not claim that markets with hidden quality always collapse; it shows a tendency that institutions like warranties, reputation, and certification routinely counteract. It is not about deliberate fraud but about the structural consequences of buyers being unable to observe quality, even with honest sellers. And signalling and screening, though closely associated with the topic, are Spence's and Stiglitz's separate contributions, not parts of Akerlof's 1970 paper, so attributing them to the original lemons analysis blurs distinct advances in the economics of information.
origin: Introduced by George Akerlof in his 1970 paper The Market for Lemons in the Quarterly Journal of Economics, showing that asymmetric information causes adverse selection; part of the work recognised by the 2001 Nobel Memorial Prize shared with Spence and Stiglitz.
